prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of a mid-size passenger airline based in Mexico D.F. The airline operates on the Hub & Spoke model and is seeking to increase its revenue. It intends to do so by switching the only airplane currently serving the flight to Mango, Brazil (an agricultural outpost) to their existing New York line service.
prompt.question: Is switching the plane from the Mango, Brazil route to the New York route a good idea?

clarifying_info.q: What type of airplane serves the Brazil line?
How many flights does the Brazil plane make per day?
What is the occupancy rate on the Brazil line?
What does a round trip ticket to Brazil cost?
How many planes currently serve the New York line?
clarifying_info.a: 4 planes, each similar to the Brazil line plane.

clarifying_info.q: How many round trips do the New York planes make per day?
clarifying_info.a: Each makes 3 round trips per day.

clarifying_info.q: What is the occupancy rate on the New York line?
What does a round trip ticket to New York cost?
What would happen to the New York occupancy rate if an additional plane is added?
clarifying_info.a: The occupancy rate would drop to 70%.

framework: Determine whether costs are relevant (they are not in this case — focus only on revenue)
Calculate current total revenue across both routes (Brazil + New York)
Calculate new total revenue if the Brazil plane is moved to the New York line
Compare new vs. current revenue to assess whether the switch improves financial performance
Consider qualitative repercussions of eliminating the Mango route (customer satisfaction, South America network effects)

questions.prompt: Calculate the current total daily revenue generated by both the Brazil (Mango) route and the New York route.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the revenue formula: seats × trips per day × occupancy rate × ticket price. Apply it separately to each route and sum. Strong candidates will note whether costs are relevant (they are not) and focus cleanly on the revenue comparison.

math.setup: Brazil revenue = seats × round trips/day × occupancy rate × ticket price. NY revenue = seats × round trips/day × number of planes × occupancy rate × ticket price.

questions.prompt: Calculate the new total daily revenue if the Brazil plane is reassigned to the New York line (now 5 planes total on NY, occupancy drops to 70%).
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply the same revenue formula to the new scenario: 5 NY planes at 70% occupancy, and zero Brazil revenue. The drop in occupancy rate is the key insight that makes the switch unattractive.

math.setup: New NY revenue = seats × round trips/day × number of planes × new occupancy rate × ticket price. Brazil revenue = $0 (route eliminated).

questions.prompt: Based on the revenue comparison, should the airline make the switch? What qualitative factors should also be considered?
questions.guidance: Candidate should clearly state that the switch decreases revenue by $63,000/day ($798k − $735k). Qualitative considerations include: loss of a high-occupancy (90%) profitable route; potential customer dissatisfaction from removing Brazil service; possible negative effects on the broader South America network via the hub-and-spoke model; and whether the capacity on the NY line is truly in demand at the projected occupancy rate.

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative repercussions might arise from eliminating the Mango, Brazil route entirely?

categories.name: Customer Impact
ideas: Loss of loyal customers on the Brazil route who may switch to competitors permanently
Damage to brand reputation in South America
Reduced customer lifetime value if Brazil-route passengers also fly on other airline routes

categories.name: Network Effects (Hub & Spoke)
ideas: Removing the Brazil leg may reduce feeder traffic into the Mexico D.F. hub
Other South American connections that rely on the Brazil route as a connecting point could be weakened
Potential domino effect on load factors for connecting flights

categories.name: Competitive Dynamics
ideas: Competitor airlines could capture the Brazil market share and strengthen their South American footprint
Client may find it costly to re-enter the Brazil market later if demand grows

categories.name: Operational Considerations
ideas: The Brazil plane has a 90% occupancy rate — it is highly utilized and profitable on its current route
Reallocating a high-utilization asset to a route that will see occupancy drop to 70% is inefficient
Maintenance and crew scheduling implications of shifting routes

recommendation: Do NOT switch the plane from the Brazil route to the New York line. The analysis shows this move would decrease total daily revenue by $63,000 (from $798,000 to $735,000).

The Brazil route, despite being served by only one plane making two round trips per day, runs at 90% occupancy and contributes $126,000/day. Eliminating it while diluting the NY line occupancy from 80% to 70% is a net loss.
risks: The NY route may not absorb the additional capacity efficiently, as evidenced by the projected occupancy drop.
Eliminating the Brazil route risks permanent loss of market share and customer goodwill in South America.
The hub-and-spoke network may be weakened if Brazil served as a feeder for other routes.
next_steps: Explore other strategies to increase revenue on the NY line without adding capacity (e.g., dynamic pricing, ancillary revenue).
Investigate whether additional demand exists for the Brazil route — if so, consider adding capacity there instead.
Assess whether any other underperforming routes exist that could be cut or consolidated without the revenue loss observed here.
